title: Water reservoir
summary: A water reservoir shown in the map legend.

enrichment.markdown:
**Water reservoir / בריכת המים**

- No outside archive located a separate record for a named reservoir under the Hebrew, Polish, Ukrainian, or English forms **בריכת המים**, *zbiornik wodny*, *rezervuar*, *vodoyem*, or *water reservoir*. The closest documented water source is **Korolowka** in Old Skala, described as the town’s main source of drinking water. Water carriers filled horse-drawn barrels there and delivered water to households; they also helped the volunteer fire brigade during fires. ([kehilalinks.jewishgen.org](https://kehilalinks.jewishgen.org/skalapodol/images/yivo%20inventory.pdf))
- The wider landscape was organized around the **Zbruch/Zbrucz River** and the smaller “potik” stream flowing into it. The surviving visual inventory places Old Skala, the Turkish castle, and the stream within the same historic landscape, suggesting that the reservoir on the map may have been a local water-management feature rather than a separately named monument. ([kehilalinks.jewishgen.org](https://kehilalinks.jewishgen.org/skalapodol/images/yivo%20inventory.pdf))

**Turkish fortress**

- The fortress was a major landmark above the Zbruch and part of Skala’s strategic border setting. The river marked the international boundary between Poland and the Soviet Union until September 1939. The archive also preserves testimony that, in July 1941, Jewish leaders were taken to the castle tower, forced to dig graves, and threatened with execution until money and goods were delivered. ([kehilalinks.jewishgen.org](https://kehilalinks.jewishgen.org/skalapodol/images/yivo%20inventory.pdf))

**Churches and civic buildings**

- The **Roman Catholic church** was described as a dominant landmark, while the **Greek Catholic church** stood farther down the hill with a roadside chapel. Both were photographed in the 1990s, confirming that these buildings or their surviving structures remained visible after the war. ([kehilalinks.jewishgen.org](https://kehilalinks.jewishgen.org/skalapodol/images/yivo%20inventory.pdf))
- The **Dom Polski** was a Polish cultural center before World War II and later became the site of the local library. The prewar **pharmacy**, **city hall**, and **post office** are likewise documented in the Skala visual inventory. ([kehilalinks.jewishgen.org](https://kehilalinks.jewishgen.org/skalapodol/images/yivo%20inventory.pdf))
- The outside material confirms the town’s changing administrative setting: Skala was in Galicia under Austria-Hungary, then Poland, Soviet Ukraine, wartime German-occupied territory, and postwar Ukraine. Yad Vashem records 1,555 Jews among 4,017 residents in the 1921 census. ([collections.yadvashem.org](https://collections.yadvashem.org/en/places/5440531))

**Rabbi’s house and Judenrat office**

- The former residence and synagogue of **Rabbi Nute Drimmer**, later used by his sons **Shlomo** and **Yehuda**, served as the **Judenrat office from July 1941 to September 1942**. This adds a precise wartime function and dates to the map’s “Rabbi’s house and Judenrat office.” ([kehilalinks.jewishgen.org](https://kehilalinks.jewishgen.org/skalapodol/images/yivo%20inventory.pdf))
- No archive result found a separate named building record for the **Gemilut Hasadim Fund**, **elementary school**, **barracks**, **police station**, or **municipality** under the spellings searched. JewishGen’s broader Skala material does, however, preserve cadastral maps from 1827–1862 and a detailed landmark/map project, making those collections the most promising route for identifying their exact plots. ([kehilalinks.jewishgen.org](https://kehilalinks.jewishgen.org/SkalaPodol/))
